subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: INDIA-CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN AIR DEFENCE MISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to inform the house that as part of the continuing effort to give help and support to India in her present difficulties, Canada is to participate in a joint commonwealth-United States air defence mission which will leave London for India on January 29 at the invitation of the Indian government. The United Kingdom and Australia will also be represented in the commonwealth component of the mission. It will examine with the Indian air force the problems it faces and the technical requirements involved in organizing an effective air defence against the possibility of any further Chinese aggression. The team includes Air Commodore Mount of the Royal Air Force, Brigadier General Tipton of the United States air force, Group Captain Murray of the Royal Canadian Air Force, and officers of the Royal Australian Air Force.
I think I should point out that the mission is of a technical nature, and that its purpose 27507-3-192J
is purely exploratory. Furthermore, no decisions will be taken by the mission, which is empowered only to report to the four sending governments. It will be up to each government to decide whether it will render assistance in improving the air defence of India and, if so, what type of assistance might be feasible. Furthermore, the sending of this mission does not imply any judgment concerning the prospects of success in the talks which may take place shortly between India and China. Whether such talks are going to take place at all is a subject which is today being debated in the Indian parliament.

subtopic: DENIAL OF ACCESS TO GOVERNMENT FILES
DENIAL OF ACCESS TO GOVERNMENT FILES
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I ask leave, seconded by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis), to move the adjournment of the house under standing order 26 for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the report made to this house by the Auditor General to the effect that he was denied access to certain files, despite the provisions of the Financial Administration Act that notwithstanding any act he is entitled to free access to all files of every department and to all the information he may deem necessary to the proper performance of his duties.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that according to standing order 26 this is the proper time on a Wednesday to raise such a motion. I am sure the house will realize that what we are discussing here, or will be if Your Honour allows the motion, is a matter which is of concern to the House of Commons. My argument that this is urgent is that an officer of the


House of Commons, responsible to us, has reported to us that he has been denied a certain right to which, by statute, he is legally entitled. I feel that at the earliest possible opportunity this matter should be discussed by the House of Commons itself.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DENIAL OF ACCESS TO GOVERNMENT FILES
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I say a word about the question of urgency of debate, which is the aspect that is in order at this moment. The house is well aware that as standard practice, a practice of long standing, with regard to either the observations or the recommendations of the Auditor General in his annual report to this house, there has been a motion introduced in this house to refer the report to the standing committee on public accounts. Then in that committee there is a detailed study with the assistance of the Auditor General, his staff and other competent witnesses, examining into the contents of the report.
It is the intention of the government to follow that normal procedure, Mr. Speaker, and to do so at the earliest possible opportunity. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, there will be afforded to the house, as well as to the public accounts committee, all the necessary or desirable freedom of discussion in relation to anything the Auditor General may have chosen to say, rightly or wrongly, on this or any other subject. I suggest, therefore, that there is no urgency of debate in relation to this matter at this time.
Important business has been announced for the house this afternoon, announced last night. This business is urgently awaiting the attention of the house and I submit, therefore, there is no justification on the ground of urgency of debate to set aside the business that has been announced for today and turn to something for which there will be ample opportunity for discussion at the earliest possible date.

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Nowlan (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DENIAL OF ACCESS TO GOVERNMENT FILES
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I have nothing to say, except that since my name is mentioned in the report I want to concur in what my colleague the Minister of Justice has said about this matter. I should like to have it fully investigated, and I hope it will be, by the public accounts committee at the earliest possible moment. It cannot be dealt with satisfactorily by a debate here, since all the records are not available. I would hope that within the next few days the officers concerned including the Auditor General, the former minister of national revenue and anyone else, will have an opportunity of appearing before that committee and dealing satisfactorily and completely with the statement which appeared in the Auditor General's report.

subtopic: DENIAL OF ACCESS TO GOVERNMENT FILES
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Finance would be quite correct if the matter being raised had to do with expenditures, which could more properly be discussed in the public accounts committee. But what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has raised is the fact that an officer of this house, responsible to this house, has been debarred from carrying out responsibilities which by public statute he is authorized and empowered to carry out. Therefore the matter now being raised is not a matter of dealing with expenditures but with a denial of the right of an officer of this House of Commons to discharge his properly allocated responsibilities. We suggest this is a matter which ought to be discussed by the house at the earliest opportunity, and that should be today.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DENIAL OF ACCESS TO GOVERNMENT FILES
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as a matter of privilege I would like to say there has been no denial. That is why I want this matter to go before a committee where evidence can be introduced and not allegations which have no foundation of fact.

subtopic: DENIAL OF ACCESS TO GOVERNMENT FILES
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in this group feel that this is a rather serious matter which has been raised, in that the Auditor General was denied access to certain files that he felt he needed to see in order to properly discharge his duties. However, we believe the proper procedure would be to refer this report to the public accounts committee at once, so that committee could call the Auditor General and other witnesses. Then when that committee reported back to the House of Commons we would know specifically what it is he thought he ought to have access to and the files to which he was denied access.
Our position is that we should have this report referred to the public accounts committee, and we urge that they take this matter up at once and call the Auditor General so that we shall know what we are talking about when we debate the matter in the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DENIAL OF ACCESS TO GOVERNMENT FILES
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is one other aspect of the matter to which I ought to have referred when addressing you earlier, and that is this. The observations of the Auditor General are contained in a report in which he reviews the public accounts for the year ended March 31, 1962. His observations do not have anything whatever to do with anything of recent occurrence or anything that is current at this moment. He is drawing attention to something which occurred during the fiscal year 1961-62, and this is another reason why this matter can be just
Motions for Papers
as properly discussed tomorrow, the next day, or at any early date as the house decides. It is not going to change its nature, its position or its condition by following the usual course.
I might say also that if the house were prepared to give unanimous consent the government would be prepared to ask the house right now to pass the motion that is annually introduced to refer the public accounts, and the report of the Auditor General thereon, to the public accounts committee for study.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: DENIAL OF ACCESS TO GOVERNMENT FILES
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Examining the proposed motion I feel that it refers to a situation which has existed for some considerable time. Further, first in view of the fact that there may be a difference of opinion as to the legal effect of the two acts and second that I also would draw attention to the point that the question that is raised must be so pressing that public interest will suffer if this matter is not given immediate attention. With the greatest respect to the hon. member I feel that, whether certain files in the hands of a ministry have or have not been examined by the Auditor General does not raise in my mind such a matter of vital interest that public interest will suffer if it is not given immediate attention.
We know that in due course the report of the Auditor General will be referred to the public accounts committee, where witnesses may be summoned and questioned, which cannot be done at this time in this house, and that opinions of legal officers may be obtained, which also cannot be done at this time in this house. Further I would urge upon hon. members the fact that this is a most extraordinary remedy, to put aside the whole business of the house to discuss a matter of this nature, in other words to suggest that there is such great urgency of debate that the rest of the business of the house must wait.
I think on both these counts this motion does not meet the requirements of section 26; therefore I cannot accept it.

Mr. Speaker, I will not take any time to argue with your ruling because what I want to say can be said within the four corners of what you have ruled. It is in order under standing order 32 to debate a motion "for reference to a committee of a report or any return laid on the table of the house." That is what I am now doing, and I am arguing that one of the reasons why this report of the Auditor General should be referred to the committee on public accounts for immediate examination is that the report brings to our attention what, in my view, is a serious interference with the rights and privileges of an officer responsible to this House of Commons.
It is not necessary for me to make any further reference to the report of the Auditor General for the purpose of making my argument, but I feel that this is the place, here on the floor of the House of Commons, where it should be drawn to the attention of the committee that we as members of the House of Commons regard this matter as very serious.
The Financial Administration Act was passed by the House of Commons, as well as by the other place, and it is on our statute books. Under the Financial Administration Act, section 65 and the sections following, the position of Auditor General is created, and one of the sections in this part of the Financial Administration Act sets out his rights in very clear language. It is section 66 (1) which says:
Nothwithstanding any act-
Please note that there are no exclusions.
-the Auditor General is entitled to free access at all convenient times to all files, documents and other records relating to the accounts of every department, and he is also entitled to require and receive from members of the public service such information, reports and explanations as he may deem necessary for the proper performance of his duties.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that that right of an officer of this house is very clear, that he has the right to have free access to all files of any department at any time, and that he has the right to require and receive whatever explanations he needs in order to pursue his duties. According to press reports the objection of the former minister of national1 revenue, the present Minister of Finance, to this request was based on a provision in the Income Tax Act. That provision is also quite clear. It is section 133 of the Income Tax Act which reads as follows:
Every person who, while employed in the service of Her Majesty, has communicated or allowed to be communicated to a person not legally entitled thereto any information obtained under this act or has allowed any such person to inspect or have access to any written statements furnished under this act is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding $200.
I submit that you do not have to have a course in law to put those two sections of those two acts together to see what they mean. The section in the Income Tax Act is the well known section regarding secrecy of information obtained by the income tax department, and it is very clear that the limitation is against giving information to anyone not legally entitled thereto. But the Auditor General is not one of the persons not entitled to such information. On the contrary, by statute passed by the House of Commons, the Financial Administration Act, he is legally entitled "notwithstanding any act" to get any information he needs to pursue his duties.
I submit therefore that what has happened is that a privilege of the House of Commons- because after all it is to the House of Commons that the Auditor General reports-has been transgressed in that an officer responsible to-the house has been denied, by a member of the cabinet, a right provided in a statute which we have passed.
As a matter of fact this denial of that right to the Auditor General has been compounded by the fact he was told, according to what he tells us, that the matter was being referred to. the Department of Justice for a ruling, but despite the lapse of considerable time he had not been advised what the ruling of the Department of Justice was. I submit that here again-

subtopic: AMENDMENTS EXTENDING APPLICATION AND INCREASING EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
On behalf of this side of the house I should like to address a few words to the committee explaining our attitude on this side in general and, if I am given the time, my own attitude in particular in connection with this amendment to the Freight Rates Reduction Act.
The purpose of the original act in 1959 was set forth by the minister in his initial statement on this matter when he told us it was to compensate shippers in western Canada and the maritimes for the 17 per cent freight rate increase which was authorized by the board of transport commissioners in 1958. As
Freight Rates Reduction Act a result of that act, a subsidy of a maximum of $20 million was authorized to allow the board to roll back the 17 per cent increase in favour of shippers, and on August 1, 1959, the board authorized a rollback from 17 per cent to 10 per cent. Later, on May 6, 1960, a rollback was made from 10 to 8 per cent. As a result, this legislation achieved a reduction for shippers in non-competitive rates of 9 per cent, that is, from 17 per cent to 8 per cent. Subsidies were paid under this act amounting to $20 million in 1959 and a further $15 million under the amendment of 1960. In 1961 there was a further $20 million; and the minister is now coming before this committee to ask for a further subsidy or third extension of $20 million, for a maximum of $75 million paid as subsidy to shippers moving traffic under commodity rates.
I should like to stress to the committee at this stage, Mr. Chairman, in order that we might analyse the effect of this extension and the effect of this act with respect to the competition between trucking and rail, that the subsidies are limited to what are known as non-competitive rates; that is to say, they are limited to commodity and class rates. The committee ought not to be confused, if I may say so with respect, over competition arising between trucking and rail, because in the main this act does not apply to rates which are made competitive by the railways in order to meet truck or water competition. A railway rate becomes competitive when the railway lowers the rate or makes a co-charge with the shipper to meet truck competition or to meet water competition. When that rate becomes competitive under the act, this subsidy does not apply. In other words, where the railways have made competitive rates in order to meet truck competition, the subsidies under this act do not go to the shippers and are not refunded to the railways.
The purpose of the amendment was outlined by the minister in his opening statement to this committee some time ago. The original act expired on April 30, 1962; and the amendment is to extend the provisions of the act to April 30, 1963. A secondary purpose is to authorize, as I have said, further subsidies of $20 million, and to authorize payment to the railways for the lower rate they have been giving shippers since April, 1962. The minister characterized this as temporary legislation which would have to do until more formal reforming legislation flowing from the MacPherson report was brought before the house. Our view of this legislation was very ably set forth by my learned friend the hon. member for Laurier

Freight Rates Reduction Act when he made his initial statement on behalf of our party at the outset of the debate before this committee. We take issue, of course, with the terminology that this is an extension of an existing act. This is a revival of an act which has already expired. In other words, at the moment, there is no legislation justifying these lower rates which shippers in western Canada and the maritimes are receiving from the railways, because the act, as I said, expired on April 30, 1962.
The railways, in accordance with an understanding with the government, have been granting the lower rates to shippers in the hope that this house will pass the amendment to the act. This is a bit of retroactive legislation to justify something which should have been done almost a year ago, and to bail the government out of a position where they will have to relieve the railways of somewhere between $15 million and $20 million paid in anticipation of legislation which at the time did not exist, nor does it now exist.
I suggest to the committee that this is just another instance, another example, of what has been happening in this house, where we are being called upon by the government to pass payments of money when it is really too late for us to do anything about it. It is seeking to bar the door when the horse has already escaped. We have had to pass interim supply which we have not seen, as well as estimates; and we are now being asked to justify payments of $20 million when most of that money has already been spent. A further extension will be needed on April 30, 1963; so that if this amendment is passed by this house in the next few days, the minister will again be obliged to come before us in about three months to ask for a further extension.
The minister said that this was temporary legislation; but it is legislation which has been renewed piecemeal year by year since
1959.	He said it is temporary legislation until the MacPherson report can be implemented. But, Mr. Chairman, the MacPherson report recommended the abolition of the present equalization policy and the abolition of the yery type of subsidy which is symbolized by this statute. In other words, the minister says: "Wait until the MacPherson report"; and the MacPherson report has recommended the abolition of this subsidy. I fail, with the greatest respect, to understand the logic behind what he says.
As my hon. friend for Laurier pointed out, this act continues to subsidize a wage increase because the motive behind it was to allow the railways the revenue with which to meet the railway employee wage increase in 1958, without similar benefit to the shippers. In


other words, the government has been put into the position where it is subsidizing a wage increase on behalf of the two railway systems of this country.
Finally, the purpose of this act should have been to benefit solely the maritimes and western shippers. But as the Canadian trucking association pointed out very conclusively, the benefits of this act are indiscriminate. Nowhere does it say which shippers are to benefit; it is limited merely to shippers moving goods under non-commodity and nonclass rates. In other words, some benefits have accrued to the central provinces when I feel sure that that was not the original purpose of the statute. If I may, Mr. Chairman, I should like to get down to the very important opposition taken to the extension of this act by the Canadian trucking association. It is an opposition which concerned every member sitting on the standing committee and gave us pause as to whether this legislation ought again to be extended. The testimony of Mr. John Magee, executive secretary of the Canadian trucking association was for me very persuasive, and from comments made to me by other members of the committee I gathered that they as well were very much impressed. The principal argument of the Canadian trucking association was that the non-competitive rates set by the railways which profit from this subsidy are really no longer non-competitive rates but would be competitive if thrown open to active competition without the benefit of a subsidy. In other words, what they said was that the present height or standard of the rate is such that it already competes with the trucking industry, and that the
Freight Rates Reduction Act trucking industry is therefore impeded in free competition because the railway is allowed to maintain an artificially low rate as a result of the subsidy.
The Canadian trucking association argues that if the present subsidy were withdrawn, many of the present so-called non-competitive rates benefiting from the subsidy would be in effect competitive rates and the railways would be forced to and would be able to reduce them. This was indicated, said Mr. Magee, by the fact that in the past three or four years the area of non-competitive rates has been steadily lowered until the non-competitive rate has become what he termed "a vanishing breed." His argument is that if this legislation were withdrawn the vanishing breed would be close to suicide and that the non-competitive rate would disappear from the traffic.
In answer to his arguments, and while admitting that there is great merit in them, I would say that if the non-competitive rate is a vanishing breed or if the non-competitive rate is disappearing, then the trucking industry has less to fear from this legislation than it had three years ago in the sense that if more and more of the rates are becoming competitive, then fewer and fewer of the rates are being subsidized and more of the rates are being opened to free competition between trucking and rail unsupported by any subsidy.
Furthermore, Mr. Chief Commissioner Kerr estimated that the trucking industry was currently carrying only 5 per cent of the goods moving under commodity and class rates. In other words, only 5 per cent of the traffic carried by the railways under the subsidized rates is being competed for by the trucks. Mr. Montague, the economic adviser to the Canadian trucking association, was unable to produce any concrete evidence to rebut that estimate, although he would put the figure closer to 10 per cent or 15 per cent. If this is so, it means that the handicaps complained of by the trucking industry in so far as this particular legislation is concerned-and I am not talking about the no-strings-attached general subsidy but only about this particular legislation-are not as great as they would have us believe. If only 5 per cent of 10 per cent of the traffic open to trucks is affected, their complaint is not as severe as they would have us believe. On the other hand, if only 5 per cent or 10 per cent of the traffic is being affected, if this House of Commons were not to pass this legislation it would mean that 90 per cent of the traffic would move from a 9 per cent rate to a 17 per cent rate because there would be no competitive trucking able to force the rate down. In other

Freight Rates Reduction Act words, shippers in western Canada or shippers in the maritimes would be forced immediately for about 90 per cent of the traffic to pay the higher 9 per cent differential.
The second argument of the trucking association was that this subsidy prolongs the railways' monopoly, and is a subsidy paid to one mode of transport to the detriment of other modes of transport, or, in other words, the subsidy is only open to shippers who use the railways; and that was the point raised by my hon. friend from Lapointe. In other words, the subsidy allows the railways, so the truckers say, to lower their rates in other areas. They say the money the railways get from the subsidies under this legislation allows them, for instance, to meet competition with trucks under agreed charges by giving them more revenue to divert into other cost factors of their operation. I suppose the answer to that might be that much of the Canadian trucking association's brief relating to this railway monopoly problem went to the general subsidy question, or to the no-strings-attached $50 million subsidy.
It would be my respectful opinion that the argument raised by the trucking association had less pertinence or less immediate application to this particular legislation. But if this subsidy is to be continued further; if the MacPherson report is perpetually to evade us in this House of Commons; if the legislation incorporating a new freight rate policy for this country is not to be brought down by the government; if the house is to be faced with a further extension of this act in three months, then the suggestion made by the trucking association last year is one which I personally find very attractive and which obviously my hon. friend from Lapointe finds attractive; namely, that the Department of Transport should investigate the possibility of transferring the application of the subsidy to the shipper, so that the shipper could choose between railway or trucking, and so that the shipper would be allowed to use the low cost mode of transport and receive the subsidy. In other words, if the purpose of the legislation is to aid the shipper and not to subsidize the railways, then to my mind it is conceivable that the shipper ought to be able to choose the mode of transport.
There is a second general comment I should like to make personally-and I stress the fact that the comment I have made about the subsidy going to the shipper rather than to the railway is my own personal comment- and that is that interprovincial and international trucking should be regulated by the same board by which railways are regulated. If, as is unquestioned, the federal government


has jurisdiction over extraprovincial or interprovincial and international trucking under the Winner case of 1954 which went to the privy council, and if at the moment the provincial transport boards are only handling this jurisdiction over interprovincial trucking because of the federal Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1954, whereby the federal government gave jurisdiction to provincial boards to handle this matter; if that is so, there would be no legal bar to the federal government again enacting legislation to assume jurisdiction over federal trucking. If the MacPherson report is to be implemented, if competition in transport is to be freed as between rail and trucking, it would seem logical that the same board ought to administer both sets of rates and both modes of transport. At the moment we have no unity and no consistency in the regulation of rail rates as opposed to the regulation of trucking. If the board of transport commissioners were to be given jurisdiction not only over rail and water transportation, as it has today, but over trucks as well, we would have a central regulatory body controlling all means of ground and water transportation.
I put this suggestion to Mr. Magee when he was before the standing committee, and his objection to it was that the trucking industry did not think that the board of transport commissioners had among its membership anybody familiar with the trucking industry. I know that many trucking people, when they do get before the board, feel that the board is weighted in favour of railways as against trucks. My suggestion to him then and to the committee now is that this would be quite simple to remedy. If the board were to be given the wider jurisdiction I suggest, it would be quite easy to appoint additional members to it who were familiar with the trucking industry. It would be a procedural point only, and I think the interests of rail, truck and water transportation could be dealt with quite fairly within the same forum. Goodness knows, we have had a proliferation of boards introduced at the present session, and if the minister were to undertake to reverse this trend of boards forever, if the minister were to institute a measure whereby federal trucking would be brought under one single board and the same board that regulates its competition, I think he would be doing a service to the country.
Our position then is that we will not oppose this legislation and the extension of the act, because if we did the dislocation to western shippers and maritime shippers would be immediately so severe as to impose serious pressure on people moving goods in those parts of the country. Second, we have a

situation where the railways have already disbursed between $15 million and $20 million to shippers under commodity and class rates covered by the subsidy in anticipation of this legislation. We have been put in the position where we are almost forced to pass it in fairness to a mode of transportation that has relied upon the government to back it up. Third, the non-competitive rates subsidized by this legislation are disappearing. As a result, the area where the subsidy operates to the detriment of the trucker is diminishing. Therefore, with a clear conscience and in the hope that more general legislation will eventually be forthcoming, we are prepared to accede to the minister's request to adopt the bill.

An hon. member says it has gone to the dogs since, and that is what I should like to bring to the attention of this house. The Canadian people first became exercised over the problem of election expenses and campaign contributions at the time of the Pacific scandal in 1873. So the new government which was elected following that scandal introduced the present legislation which has been in effect ever since. My submission is that the statute is now sadly in need of reform. I will not go into detail here but I doubt if there is a responsible group, or even if there is a responsible person, in public life in Canada opposed to the first two proposals which I suggest should be submitted to the standing committee on privileges and elections. Certainly, there is no responsible newspaper in Canada objecting to these two needed reforms. The Brantford Expositor, the Toronto Globe and Mail and the Toronto Star among many newspapers have been pressing for electoral reform along these lines. In addition, well known newspaper columnists such as Mr. Blair Fraser and others have been pointing out the inadequacy of the present law for a number of years. Canadian political leaders of various parties have been crying for reform. The Hon. C. G. Power, now a member of the Senate, has been a leader in this regard. He introduced a bill which reached this house-a bill known as the political expenditures bill-in 1939, containing sweeping provisions for reform-provisions which required the publication both of the income and expenditure of political parties and limiting the amount of expenditure of candidates 27507-3-1934
Canada Elections Act
to 20 cents per voter plus $1,000 for the personal expenses of candidates.
Mr. Power described this measure at the time as a businesslike piece of legislation which would bring about open disclosure to the public, a disclosure such as would be made in the operation of private business.
In 1948, Mr. Power admitted that his bill was laughed at at the time it was introduced, and that its objectives were ridiculed as being academic and unrealistic. But he brought the same measure before this house in 1949 and it passed second reading without one single voice of dissent. It did not proceed further because parliament was dissolved and a general election called. Thus, today we have the same law as we have had since 1874, the law which has been complained about so much. The same situation exists and nothing has been done about it since.
It is now 1963 and I am asking this house of minorities at least to permit the standing committee to discuss this much needed reform. I notice that at Christmas time Mr. Power had completed 45 years of public life in Canada. I think it would be a nice thing if this house could at least consent to consideration being given to these matters by the committee as some recognition of a long life devoted to the public service of Canada.
Now I come to the third suggested amendment-that provision be made for the payment out of general revenue of the legally permitted election expenditures of those candidates who receive a reasonable percentage of the total votes cast in each constituency.
As I stated in my speech on the motion of the hon. member for York South, this third proposal is a little more controversial, but 1 maintain it is sound.
There was a debate in this house in the year 1920 on electoral reform. In that debate that much-revered Canadian statesman, the Hon. W. S. Fielding, stated that the only real solution to excessive and improper election expenditures was to make all such expenditures of sums a charge on the federal treasury. He predicted in that debate that the day would come when this House of Commons would pass such legislation. I know that on this third proposal there will be a cry of: "Oh, election expenses in Canada will rise to an unprecedented figure". But I maintain that the Canadian people are paying the bills for election expenditures at the present time in many ways: by their own private contributions, and by the rise in the cost of goods as a result of companies giving large sums of money, donating large sums to the election campaigns and expenditures of the various political parties.
I think it is true to say that today the contributions to election campaign expenditures

Canada Elections Act
are largely from big contributors, and the sum contributed in small contributions amounts to very little. In the United States, President John Fitzgerald Kennedy, two weeks after he was elected, stated that work should be started at once on legislation to provide for payment out of the United States treasury of the presidential election campaign expenditures so that, to quote him, "We can discontinue having candidates going around with their hats in their hands". In Canada, the Brantford Expositor took exception to this third reform which I have mentioned in a leading article; but the Toronto Globe and Mail did not take that view, and the Toronto daily Star complimented me upon bringing to the house a proposal for a much-needed and long-overdue reform. I stated a few moments ago that the percentage of contributions from small contributors amounted to very little. The overwhelming amount of contributions comes from big companies and big labour unions, and I say to this house that this situation is not of the best and could be dangerous. In the province of Quebec legislation has already been passed, which did not come into effect before the last provincial election, covering all of these items which I have asked this House of Commons to refer to its standing committee.
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to talk at length or to prolong my remarks, because others will want to speak and I should like to hear their views upon the question. But before taking my seat I should like to say that I know all members of this House of Commons are jealous of the sovereign rights and independence of the parliament of Canada, because each year a mass of legislation is passed through this house which affects the life of every Canadian. I should like to state that at the present time many Canadian companies have huge lumps of capital invested on the part of foreign investors, and when large contributions are made to political parties they can also be accompanied by sponsorship of a type of legislation that is not in the best interests of the sovereignty of Canada or of the independence of parliament. Keeping this in mind-and it is a very important point- I believe that this house could do well to pass these suggestions on for consideration and more prolonged discussion, at this point of time in this year 1963, to the standing committee on privileges and elections. I believe that they will be for the betterment of Canada, for the preservation of democratic principles, and for the continuance of the sovereignty of this house and of our country.

Mr. Speaker, I must congratulate the

hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Brown) who introduced this motion to amend the act respecting election expenditures.
In the province where I come from, we know something about that. I do not know how an election is run in the other provinces across Canada, I have never seen one. Nor do I wish to unduly disparage my own province, but in Quebec, people are beginning to think that an election is the occasion of a huge treat. That should have been corrected long before 1963.
I was told that the present Quebec government was preparing an amendment to the act in order to grant to each party an amount proportionate to the number of votes obtained. Frankly, when you look at the report on election expenditures, after seeing some members at work during an election-and I would not wish to charge anyone with committing perjury-you would think they have very rickety adding machines.
When one sees the tremendous electoral machine at work in some ridings, one wonders if that is not tantamount to a lack of civilization. The electoral machine has an extraordinary influence on public opinion. In fact, it is even used to attack public men in their private lives. Another thing, candidates promise things they know they will never give. That is the harm that representatives do to Canadian politics.
I went through an election for the first time. The member for Brantford said that he is not ready to pass the hat. Well unfortunately I am one of those who had to pass the hat. But there is one good side to that: I showed in my return the correct amount of money I spent for election purposes, as I did not have to lie to arrive at a reasonable figure.
As the hon. member for Brantford stated, parties should report the sources of their income because foreigners are trying to influence our country's politics by contributing to the campaign funds of our political parties. People wonder why foreigners have so much power. It is because certain political parties have their hands tied by power-happy individuals. This is something that should have been discussed long before 1963 but since we are now dealing with this matter, we must take every means at our disposal to correct this situation which has done so much harm to this country.
If, as the hon. member for Brantford who sponsored the motion claims, this state of things is, as I presume, a danger to Canada, I gladly support the motion because this situation has to be corrected. In my opinion,

the whole house is duty bound to do so, because it is the first step toward the great political clean-up which must be made in order to have basically honest politics. I do not tax politics with complete dishonesty; but, to say the contrary, I should be obliged to stretch the truth a little. If political parties could balance their electoral budgets, I think they would be less reluctant to declare their sources of income.
In any case, I am talking on behalf of my own party. We were considered as beggars, but we do not owe anything to anyone. We only promised to give the best of ourselves. We have entered politics in full freedom and have acted accordingly. This is true of every single member of our party. It has been said that the situation was worse in provincial elections than in federal elections. But there is one thing we are beginning to realize in the province of Quebec, and it is that federal elections also are expensive. Federal political parties are taking the lead from provincial ones. Bad example does strange things.
Yet, it is the Canadian government who should set the example. That is why, it should be its duty to have some piece of legislation adopted, including provision to the effect, for instance, that elections should be held honestly, so that those who take part in them may remain honest. In other words, the example must come from Ottawa.
There would be much more to say on the matter, but other members probably wish to take the floor.
I have no doubt that the motion introduced by the hon. member will be carried. Therefore, may I close my remarks by saying that before rejecting this motion, we should consider it dispassionately in the interests of all Canadian citizens.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on this motion one immediately realizes that what is being asked here has been asked on a number of different occasions down through the years. The question of elections and election expenses has come up for consideration in this house once already in this session and perhaps in a
Canada Elections Act
number of other sessions. Here we are being asked to refer certain conditions to a standing committee for the purpose of studying them and perhaps coming up with the solution suggested by the mover of this motion or perhaps disagreeing with it.
In the first place, the mover of the motion is asking us to limit expenditures in all Canada to an effective ceiling, whatever that effective ceiling may be. Whether he is trying to control or to limit people or whether he is trying to make it broad enough to include all the big spenders in his party and perhaps ours, I do not really know. However, I would suggest that the words "effective ceiling" could be debated for some hours before any figure could be arrived at.
He also would like to bring about a strict system of accounting for expenditures. I suggest this would be a very difficult thing to do as one never knows when one is making an expenditure on behalf of another in politics. For example, I as a candidate may have a flat tire and may have some farmer drive me to a campaign meeting. He may do this free of charge. He may be contributing to my election expenses. I do not know whether or not this item would have to be put in this strict accounting. Again, if some big company thought that my views or his views were right and came into the constituency and spent a great deal of money on that campaign without the person even asking for it, I do not know whether this money would be included as an expenditure in the campaign. It would be something which would be very hard to determine. In my opinion, it would be nearly impossible.
Last of all, his suggestion is to provide for the payment of all election expenses of candidates who secure a reasonable portion of the votes in a constituency. That is another matter which I think it would be very difficult for any deciding judge or any ruling body to determine. Certainly if we had a system such as that to which he referred in the United States or which was referred to in President Kennedy's remarks with regard to election expenses, or a system something similar to theirs where they have nearly got down to a two party system-while it is not statutory, that is in a sense what is operating there-then I might see the feasibility and the possibility of the government standing some or all of the expenditures of the candidate. However, in our country, anybody in a constituency, if he meets the conditions set out in the elections act with regard to being a Canadian citizen and has residence of the required time before the election is called, can become a candidate in that constituency. He does not have to belong to any given political party. He may even found his own

Canada Elections Act
party and run, as a particular candidate did in my constituency in the 1962 election. Perhaps he felt he received a reasonable share of the vote. In his thinking maybe this was all he expected in the first year of founding his political party. I do not know about that.
I never asked him. However, that may have been what he thought was a reasonable start.
Certainly the idea of a reasonable amount of anything could be subject to a great deal of question. The only other reference I know of with regard to "reasonable" is in the grain act under the grading of grain. If I am right and if I may refer to it for a moment, may I say that as to the definition of reasonable I think the grain act states that No. 2 wheat is to be reasonably free of weed seeds and immature kernels; and I am told by the board of grain commissioners that this deals with a figure of 5 per cent. No. 1 wheat, according to the terms of the grain act is to be practically free of immature kernels and weed seeds and No. 2 wheat shall be reasonably free of immature kernels; and they consider that 5 per cent or something near that figure of 5 per cent meets the requirement. Would 5 per cent be a reasonable percentage of the votes of a constituency? I do not know what the hon. member is referring to here. I point out this consideration. The matter could be subject to a great deal of controversy with regard to paying election expenses. With regard to limiting expenditures certainly one would have to take into consideration many things such as the locality of the constituency; the number of miles one is obliged to cover; whether it is all populated or whether it is partially populated; whether it covers a rough terrain as it would if a portion of it were in the Rocky mountains; and I can think of several in Alberta which are in the Rocky mountains; or whether it be in the Northwest Territories or the Yukon. Certainly those constituencies are much more difficult to campaign in. As years go on and as improvements in transportation take place and as those areas become more settled candidates will be obliged to spend more and more money in those areas. Perhaps private aeroplanes and the hiring of them will become more common. However, I suggest that they will be still very expensive and that many areas must be covered in that way.
I can certainly understand the situation with regard to a city riding which includes so many blocks west of Main street and so many blocks east of Main street and is a neat little parcel with many people living in it who are easy to get in touch with over one radio station perhaps, and in one daily newspaper. I can understand the feasibility of limiting expenses in a riding of that type. However,

ridings of that type while perhaps not in the minority I am sure are not in the majority in this vast country of ours today.
I was in some ways interested in the remarks of the hon. member from the Social Credit party. From the way in which he started out I thought for a while he was against this particular measure. However, he corrected my wrong impression by stating that he would second the motion and strongly wished it to carry. This is an interesting viewpoint to be expressed by that particular party, because as one who comes from Alberta I know that the people there have seen numerous parties in that province rise and fall. I can think of the ginger group as it was commonly called which was elected in the twenties, the old U.F.A. government that operated there in the twenties and part of the thirties, and the present Social Credit government in that province.
If there were a system whereby the government paid part of the expenses of all candidates who received a reasonable share of the votes and if the number of candidates allowed to enter any campaign were in any way limited, one can readily see that various parties would never come out of the eggshell, shall I say. Even the Social Credit party might never have come into being in 1935 if such a system had been in existence because the government then might very well not have paid part of their election expenses and might very well have not even recognized them as having a possible chance. Certainly in the early founding days of that party they themselves must have wondered about this. I suppose they are no longer wondering, of course, because they have become established. However, they are trying desperately now to bring about a resurgence after having fallen on evil days.
I use this as an example. Certainly we cannot limit the number of candidates who may want to run in any given election. The hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Brown) referred to basic democratic principles and if we accept this as one of our basic democratic principles how can we as a government say that we will pay part or all of the election expenses of candidates as long as they receive a reasonable share of the votes? There might very well be a large number of candidates wishing to run in any given constituency and this could involve the expenditure of a great deal of money.
If there were a sufficiently large number of candidates this would eventually put a limit on the amount any one candidate could spend because there is only so much money to go around under today's conditions. Maybe if we started to print money, as some would

like us to do, there might be more. The hon. member for Brantford said in his closing remarks that we must guard our democratic principles; however I cannot support this motion because it leaves too many things undecided.
To sum up briefly, this effective ceiling about which he talks is a very mythical figure. I would hesitate to guess what it might be. In the last campaign I think I spent an average amount. Possibly that average would be taken as the ceiling in order to place a limit on expenditures in some of the constituencies where vast amounts were spent. I do not know. Maybe you would take the constituency where the most money was spent and use that figure as the limit. I do not know what is meant by an effective ceiling and I suggest there could be a good deal of debate on that point. I suggest that at no time would we all agree on what an effective ceiling should be. I think this is an elusive amount which would grow and grow as the years went by.
We can only refer to election costs in past years. For example, in the 1949 election total election expenditures by the various parties were a little over $2 million. In 1958 total election expenditures were substantially over $3 million and I suppose that at the present time such expenditures might well approach $4 million. The figure is going up all the time. The effective ceiling would have to be increased, I suggest, having in mind the urge that politicians have to get in touch with everybody in their riding and leave no hand unshaken and no door on which they have not knocked. As communications improve politicians will have an increasing urge to knock on every door and shake every hand. Therefore I suggest that election expenses will continue to rise and if an effective ceiling could be arrived at today it would not be suitable four years from now or eight years from now or at any other time.
The other point has to do with a strict accounting of such expenditures. I firmly believe that in an election a strict accounting is practically impossible. Let us be practical. Let us consider what is being suggested here and whether a committee of this house or the house itself should pass upon it or spend time debating it. A strict accounting of election expenses would be a very difficult thing to achieve because it would have to take into account everything that my neighbours or my good friends spent on my behalf. Every time they even talked to their neighbours or knocked on a few doors on my behalf any expense involved would have to be included.
Canada Elections Act
I do not really know just what would have to be included, but there are many ways of getting around the carrying out of a strict accounting. I can remember a provincial election a few years ago in which I took a great deal of interest although I was not a candidate. I thought to myself that the sitting member was spending a terrific amount of money in that campaign and that there was a great deal of fanfare. His name was on the radio all the time and there was a great deal of fanfare in the local and weekly papers, including full page advertisements. I thought to myself that I would like to see his expense account when he published it after the election but, much to my surprise, when it came out the figure was very low. In fact, I think he had only spent a thousand dollars or so, according to the report in the paper.
I met him after the election and as I was on reasonably friendly terms with him I said, "How is it that your expenses were so low? I thought you were really burning up the money during that campaign?" He said, "That was not I; that was the party headquarters. That money was not spent by me at all."
These are questions that arise in my mind when I consider whether a strict accounting is possible. I think it would be practically impossible. I have dealt with the question of a reasonable proportion of the votes cast and the question of paying a part of the election expenses. I feel it would be very difficult to arrive at a reasonable proportion. If one wanted to, he could arrive at a reasonable proportion but it would definitely limit the number of candidates in a particular riding. It is all well and good to quote what President Kennedy said two days after he was elected, but I think it is more pertinent to inquire what he has said about the matter since. I have not seen that he has said anything about election expenses since. One can say a great many things two days after being elected or two days before but it does not take very long after being elected to become burdened with the cares of office, and perhaps this tends to make one's thinking a bit more reasonable and practical.
In this country where we have no limit on political parties or on the number of candidates who run in a particular constituency, I feel that the government in governing the country cannot accept the idea that the government should pay part or all of the election expenses, no matter what proportion of the votes we arrive at as being reasonable. If we wish to guard our democratic principles then I think we must not carry out any of the ideas suggested in this motion. I see no reason

Mr. Speaker, I rise to express the views of the New Democratic party on the resolution that the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Brown) has put before the house. We look upon this resolution as one which has a twofold purpose. It provides for the payment of election expenditures out of public funds and it imposes a ceiling upon election expenditures by candidates. In our view these things are important but, Mr. Speaker, we will not have an effective electoral law and we will not adequately reform our electoral system until we provide for complete disclosure of the sources of campaign funds. I agree, and I think all the members in all parties agree, that the present system badly needs to be changed.
I recall reading a few months ago an article in Maclean's magazine by James Scott, once a federal organizer for the Liberal party, who candidly revealed what went on in the Liberal and Conservative parties in connection with fund raising. He pointed out that when one of these parties was in office the people who received government contracts, corporations which received favours from the government, would allocate a certain amount of money for electoral purposes and would distribute 60 per cent of it to whichever of the old-line parties was in office and 40 per cent to whichever party was out of office. They met their campaign budgets rather effectively in those days, and no doubt they are still doing so.
The hon. member for Brantford believes, I take it, that if his party were to get into office again, which seems rather unlikely, they would change our electoral system to conform with the worth-while objectives found in his resolution. I am not aware of the policy of the Liberal party and whether it conforms to his resolution, but perhaps the leader of the Liberal party will change it overnight, as he has done with other policies espoused by the Liberal party. At the moment, however, Liberal policy remains in the same state of confusion, remains shrouded in the mist that surrounds not only Liberal party policy but apparently the leader of that party as well.

I gave up long ago reading Liberal propaganda because if the platform that is in the pamphlet the hon. member has waved on high is going to be carried out in the same way his party carried out its promise to introduce a national health insurance scheme back in 1919, then I think the point in reading his propaganda is lost-at least, that is the way it looks to me.
Let me deal with two matters that were raised by the resolution of the hon. member. He said that a payment should be made out of public funds to candidates securing a reasonable proportion of the total votes cast. This would discriminate against third parties in some of the provinces of Canada. The hon. member who just spoke pinpointed this difficulty I thought rather well. If the decision as to the reasonable proportion were to be left in the hands of some agency, some political group or some government which fixed it at such a high level third parties could not gain any advantage from the measure, this would present a serious difficulty.
In British Columbia, the Liberal party might be discriminated against because it is a third party there. In Newfoundland the Conservative party might be discriminated against because I understand that in that province every party except the party in power is a third party. In Ontario, the Social Credit party must be regarded as a third, fourth or fifth party, and perhaps it would be discriminated against. Let me point out that legislation which in principle was sound, put forward some time ago by the premier of Quebec, to reform the electoral system in his province, was legislation which discriminated against third parties. I think all of us were pleased to hear that apparently that legislation is going to receive further consideration before it is put before the legislature of that province.
Now, the hon. member also suggests in his resolution that there should be strict accountability for all expenditures of each candidate. This is important, that candidates should be accountable. However, we should keep in mind that under our present electoral system they are accountable. But it is not enough to make candidates accountable. Parties that contest federal elections are organized on a federal basis, and the federal organization of each party must be accountable. I gather, from what Mr. Scott has said, it is the federal organization which gets the funds which enable some parties to charter jetliners for their leaders to travel around the country. It is the federal party which pays for the

slick supplements in Sunday supplements and other newspapers which are used in federal election campaigns. It is the federal party which makes use of the Madison avenue techniques which inundate the population of this country with tons of political claptrap at election time.
Some of us wondered, as a matter of fact, when parliament opened, why the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson), even before parliament had opened, said that he wanted an election right away. He felt that the idea of an election was not to elect a parliament, but that you elected a parliament in order to have an election. At any rate, we wondered why he did not even wish to come into this house to hear what the government was going to put forward. The members of this party, like the members of the Liberal party, were disappointed when we heard what the government put before us. But we wondered why the Liberal leader did not wish even to come to parliament to hear it. We wondered why he did not wish to test the mettle of his colleagues in this house where, after all, we are all equal. We do not have to depend on chartered jetliners, the slick Sunday supplements; we do not have to rely on editorialists to whip themselves up into a frenzy of support.
My point is that the federal organization of each party must be made strictly accountable, not just the candidates themselves. If the candidate's funds are raised at the local level by small donations from various individuals in the local community, from local trade unions or local businessmen, then certainly the candidate's expenses will be disclosed under our elections act. But only that portion of the party's expenses which is raised at the local level will under those circumstances be disclosed, and the enormous amounts of money that, as James Scott has told us, are provided to the old-line parties at the federal level will not be accounted for. It is for this reason that the necessity for the full disclosure of election campaign expenses is, to some extent, not taken into account by this measure.
One of the members of this party put forward a resolution during the fall sitting of parliament proposing that certain of the expenses of candidates be paid for out of public funds. The hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) proposed that certain use of public news media be made available to candidates, that transportation expenses should be taken care of by the federal government, and that the expense of producing at least one piece of election literature be paid for out of public funds.
I think all of us would agree this is perhaps a better way to approach the problem than 27507-3-194
Canada Elections Act
simply to provide a lump sum payment out of public funds, because this at least ensures that the public would not be put to the expense of providing political claptrap. The public will only be put to the expense of providing a useful, sensible and rational means of propagating the ideas espoused by each of the political parties.
I myself believe it is time in this country for parliament to consider establishing the equivalent of the C.B.C. in the newspaper field. The C.B.C. has worked in the field of broadcasting and television, and there is no reason why that concept cannot work in the field of the dissemination of news and public information by the press. Such an institution could be made available in the same way as free time broadcasts are made available at present to candidates, in order to enable them to put their platforms and policies before the public.
Politics is the public's business. I ask what good are democratic rights if only the wealthy can exercise them? What freedom of choice has the voter when it is only those candidates in those political parties with large resources available to them who can reach him with their messages? What freedom of choice can he have under those circumstances? How can the Canadian government be above suspicion, how can any party serve its country to the utmost, when the source of its funds is shrouded in a cloak of secrecy?
The hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Brown) has brought forward a motion proposing that public funds be made available to candidates for public office, and which would establish a ceiling on the amount of expenditures which could be made by any candidate for public office. Subject to the important reservations I have made that third parties should be not discriminated against, and that there should be an accounting at all levels, including the federal level, of election campaign expenses, I think the motion is sound and the members of this party will support it when the vote is called, as I am confident it will be during the next few minutes.
It is estimated that during the last election campaign more than $12 million was spent on election expenses, both at the federal level and by individual candidates, by the four parties sitting in this house. If the public were to undertake the expense involved in election campaigns and thereby obtain honesty in government and honesty in public administration, and achieve a situation where public administration could be removed from any taint of suspicion, it would be a small price to pay to bring honesty into the conduct of election campaigns in Canada and into the administration of public business.

Mr. Speaker, unfortunately the shortness of time prevents me from dealing first with the largely irrelevant innuendoes just offered by the last speaker, but I would like to address a few remarks to certain statements made by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Horner).
I rise to speak in favour of the motion and would like to elaborate to some degree the attitude of this party to the proposal, and particularly to some of the questions raised by the hon. member for Acadia. His first and major objection was to the question of an effective ceiling on election expenses. He suggested in some way it would not be humanly possible to arrive at a proper effective ceiling for that purpose.
I would like to draw the attention of hon. members to the experience of other countries in the western world, and France in particular, where this kind of calculation has been found possible and the system has been satisfactory for many years. I recognize, however, there are problems in calculating such an effective ceiling caused not only by the topography of a particular riding, which was the kind of thing the hon. member referred to, but also problems caused by areas with which he may not be so familiar; and I speak of running an election campaign in large metropolitan centres. One of the problems is the hiring of space and media, and in the case of Toronto a candidate may pay full price for only one eighteenth of the coverage of a particular media.
These are the kinds of problems which could most effectively be dealt with by a committee, and it is for this reason that the hon. member for Brantford has suggested that the matter be referred to a committee where it can be fully studied. The committee can consider statements by those most experienced in this field and can also call on the services of experts in the field of political science.
The hon. member for Acadia raised problems with regard to the strict accountability of expenses. While I acknowledge the example he cited of a neighbour assisting him with a flat tire, and agree it may be difficult to account for that in election expenses, it is no different from the problem we have encountered with income tax in determining small contributions and donations which should come into income but which are difficult to account for. But, the difficulty of accounting for such particular sums has not prevented us from levying income tax.
With respect to the suggestion that the motion should refer only to those candidates who obtain a reasonable proportion of the total votes cast, I would make the suggestion that instead of having such a vague requirement, an arbitrary measure be put into the elections act providing that every candidate who gets 20 per cent of the votes cast will have his expenses met in this way. We already have a precedent in that act, in an equally arbitrary measure with regard to deposits.

speechtext: I was going to inquire from whoever is leading the house, and I take it it is the Minister of Defence Production, if he could indicate to the house what the business will be for Thursday and Friday?
There is no change in the program. We will deal with external affairs estimates tomorrow, and Friday with national defence.

speechtext: Could the acting house leader give any indication what the business would be for next week?
I was told by the house leader just a moment ago that he will announce it tomorrow night.
At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.

subtopic: FURTHER CORRESPONDENCE RESPECTING AMENDMENT OF B.N.A. ACT

speechtext:
(Translation):
Ottawa, January 3rd 1963.
My dear Premier,
In your letter of September 19th, in reply to mine of August 27th regarding the proposed amendment to section 94A of the British North America Act, you stated that, since the Quebec legislature had been dissolved, you felt it preferable to wait until it met again before going further into the matter.
You will be interested to know that I have now received a letter, dated December 11th, in which the premier of Newfoundland agrees to the proposed amendment to section 94A. Thus all provinces, save Quebec, have now signified concurrence in this amendment.
May I now take the liberty of expressing the hope that Quebec will join her nine sister provinces in support of the proposed amendment. It seems to me that the measure has become even more urgent since your last letter.
Yours sincerely,
John G. Diefenbaker.
The hon. Jean Lesage,
Premier of the Province of Quebec,
Quebec, P.Q.
OFFICE OF THE PREMIER Province of Quebec
January 8th, 1963.
My dear Prime Minister,
In reply to your letter of January 3rd, I must say that I see no reason to change the position I took in my letters to you of January 24th and February 8th, 1962 with regard to Section 94A of the British North America Act.
At the time the provinces were asked their assent to the constitutional amendment of 1951 regarding Old Age pensions, the federal government had given them definite information on the nature of the legislation it was planning to enact. Now, on the contrary, we are given only the vaguest of indications which do not allow us to determine the implications of the unexplicit text we are asked to accept.
27507-3-194J
I must therefore repeat that I find it impossible to introduce a proposed constitutional amendment in the legislature unless I have on hand the particulars of your project.
I intend to table in the house a copy of your last letter, together with this reply, as soon as the next session opens on Tuesday the 15th.
Yours sincerely,
Jean Lesage.
The Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker,
Prime Minister of Canada,
Parliament Buildings,
Ottawa.
(Text):
Ottawa, December 24th, 1962. The Honourable J. R. Smallwood, M.H.A., Premier of Newfoundland,
St. John's, Newfoundland.
My dear Premier,
I acknowledge and thank you for your letter of December 11 in which you advise that the government of Newfoundland have no objection to the proposed amendment to section 94A of the British North America Act, which would allow parliament to legislate in relation not only to old age pensions, but also in relation to pensions and other benefits incidental to, and conducive to the better operation and administration of, a scheme of old age pensions.
You ask that your administration be advised of the nature of the legislation which the government of Canada proposes to introduce and you suggest that this was done in 1951 when the present clause 94A was added to the British North America Act. According to my information, although there was consultation between the federal and provincial governments at that time it did not result in any effort to provide or request detailed information on the legislative measures that were to follow the adoption of the constitutional amendment.
With respect to your request that you be advised as to how soon, after the concurrence cf the governments of all the provinces

is secured, it is proposed to introduce the legislation into parliament, I would say that after the address has been passed by the Canadian parliament and the British North America Act amendment has been passed at Westminster then we will be in a position to introduce legislation.
Yours sincerely,
"Original signed by John G. Diefenbaker".
The government of the province of Newfoundland
THE PREMIER St. John's
11 December, 1962
Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker, M.P., Prime Minister of Canada,
Ottawa.
My dear Prime Minister:
My colleagues and I have now had an opportunity to give consideration to the proposal made originally in your letter of January 27, 1962 and renewed in a letter of August 25 for the concurrence of the governments of the provinces in a proposed amendment to section 94A of the British North America Act to provide explicitly that the parliament of Canada should be authorized to legislate not merely with respect to old age pensions but also with respect to pensions
and other benefits incidental to, or conducive to the better operation and administration of a scheme of old age pensions.
We are wholly sympathetic to the idea of incorporating in any contributory old age security legislation provisions for the payment of benefits to widows and children of contributors and to contributors who become permanently disabled. While our government is inclined to review that the present section 94A might provide sufficient legislative authority for such legislation we see no objection to an explicit reference in the constitution which would remove all doubt on this score.
We recall that when the original amendment was made in 1951 to include section 94A the provincial governments were advised of the nature of the legislation the government of Canada proposed to introduce in parliament and we would hope that a similar courtesy would be extended by your administration in the present circumstance. We would also appreciate being advised as to how soon after the concurrence of the governments of all the provinces is secured it is proposed to introduce the legislation into parliament.
Meanwhile this letter is to advise you that the government of Newfoundland have no objection to the proposed amendment.
Sincerely yours, Joseph R. Smallwood.
Thursday, January 24, 1963
